What an extraordinary meal.  Yes it's expensive and yes the portions are small. But portions in France are typically smaller than American portions so that's what we expected. But each and every dish we had was exquisite.  Everything was perfectly presented with a beautiful sauce.  Service was excellent except took too long for the check.  Our favorite was the Sweetbreads.  We were lucky enough to sit by the kitchen where we got to watch the large staff painstakingly prepare each dish with Chef and owner Daniel Rose at the helm. 
Our only issue and recommendation is that they offer more wines under  $100.  Almost all the wines were quite expensive and priced 4 times retail.

After my meal, I've named this place Le Doo Doo or Le Poo Poo (your choice).  Went for Valentines Day and was not impressed.  My entree was the sole with spinach and it was WAY TOO BUTTERY and used TOO MUCH HEAVY CREAM.  I ended up barely making my way through half of it before I couldn't take it anymore.  We also ordered the grilled venison filet which I thought was OK, nothing special.  The gratin of celeri was also way too buttery and used a lot of heavy cream.

The service was mediocre at best for a restaurant of this caliber.  For example, when I sat down, there was no convenient place to put my clutch so that I could sit in the chair comfortably; they didn't even offer me a small stool to put my clutch on, I had to ask them for a hook.  Also, in the midst of our meal, a fork flew under my seat from god knows where, but it was b/c the wait staff mishandled it.

The positives were the desserts, extensive wine selection and music in the bathroom.

if you're looking for solid french food, take a visit to Gabriel Kreuther across from Bryant Park, much more worth your calories, energy and cost.

Love the ambience of this place. Seems like every table is set with a new foot-long candle which adds to the atmosphere, be it romance or frivolity. Ironically we didn't order one poultry dish- we ordered two different fish dishes which were good but not $40 good. The glasses of wine were exorbitant as well at $19 a pop. I'd say good experience once, impeccable service but plenty of other options if you want bang for your buck.

The food at le coucou is absolutely delicious, simple yet elegant. I had the lobster salad and the halibut. Both were very tasty and I left nothing on my plate. 

The restaurant itself is very beautiful, warm, cozy, and charming. I particularly enjoyed their cocktails which are some of the best in lower Manhattan.

Wow! We had a perfect dinner. The restaurant is beautiful, chic and casual. The service is very friendly and professional, attentive but not overbearing. The food lives up to the hype and exceeded our expectations. Every dish was perfectly executed with great ingredients and amazing flavors. French cuisine at its best: very rich and flavorful but managing to stay light and letting the quality of the ingredients shine. 
I highly recommend every dish we had: the Crepe with crab meat, the sweetbreads, the Halibut and the filet de bœuf.
We were really excited for this meal because we ate at Daniel's other restaurant the year before Spring and loved it. This meal was just ok nothing really blew me out of the water.

Imagine you want to take out your parents or your SO's parents, or you just have a special occasion - this place is the place for you. From space and service to the wax-candle lit table setting, le coucou screams special occasion with special people. 

Food is french at its utmost core - luxurious and rich, but delicious regardless. 

Can't think of a next time I'll be back but it will be on top of the recommendation list for me

Service here is some of the best that I have ever received. I was clearly under dressed considering I had gotten reservations on a whim the day before my arrival. I checked in to my hotel and got lunch and walked around the city for a little bit and before we knew, it was time for our dinner reservations at 5:45. 

When we arrived, they asked us for our coats and umbrellas which was so nice. Shortly after, we were taken to our table. The servers are extremely attentive and it is a wee bit annoying as it takes away from the ambiance, the solitude you want in such a beautiful environment. We skipped the appetizers and proceeded to dinner as we were still sort of full from eating around the city.

I had all of the rabbit and it was very good. I won't go much into detail about the flavor profile as everyone has talked about it to death on here. The other dish was the monkfish/lobster broth one and it was absolutely phenomenal. It was a wee bit salty but I really feel like it needed to be + it could have easily been shared between the two. I couldn't even finish all of my food. The dessert that my cousin got was absolutely delicious. 

The sommelier suggested that we get the pinot noir from the Irancy region which would pair well with our dishes. Overall, I was very satisfied with the service and the food was generally good. I just wasn't blown out of the water for how much we paid. Why I took off a star is because making reservations for this place was such a hassle.

I had been dying to come here for a while and finally got my wish on a recent Monday night (after making a reservation a month in advance). My boyfriend and I arrived at 6:15 and were promptly ushered to our table, which was a two-top against a wall, so we only had people on one side of us. A win, for sure. That said, the restaurant is so cavernous that it doesn't feel cramped at all. It's a beautiful space.

We wanted to sample a decent number of things from the menu without going nuts, so we settled on:

--Salade de betteraves au vinaigre de cidre (roasted beets, smoked eel, crème fraîche)
--Crêpe "souvenir de Lannilis" (crab, buckwheat, lime)
--Ris de veau a l'estragon (sweetbreads, crème de tomate, tarragon)
--'Choucroute' à la juive (for two) (duckling, foie gras, daikon radish prepared Alsatian style)
--Crêpe soufflé au citron (lemon ice cream, citron confit)

I loved the beets even though I normally don't like smoked foods. Oddly, my boyfriend, who loves smoked things, thought it was too smoky. I found the crab dish to be too limey, but my boyfriend loved it. The sweetbreads were amazing. I'd never had them before, but wanted to try them and was not disappointed. Very rich and reminiscent of fois gras in texture. The duckling for two was phenomenal: duck breast, duck leg confit, duck heart, fois gras, and fermented radish. The latter was like a sauerkraut but better. The confit essentially melted in our mouths. Delicious all the way around. I normally don't love lemon desserts, but the soufflé was light and perfect, especially after the heavier meat dishes.

My boyfriend and I each had the In Memoriam to drink (gin, cynar, rooibos, oleo saccharum), which was very unique and complex. I also had a gin mule that was expertly mixed.

In total, the bill came to 300 bucks (with tip), which seemed reasonable given everything we ordered and the quality. We're definitely looking forward to returning!

Our lunch at Le Coucou was a nice respite from the busy Manhattan weekend of subway construction and traffic. Entering the dining room of vaulted ceilings and chandeliers, I felt I was in a former bank building. Surprisingly, this was a former Holiday Inn for budget tourists who wanted to stay in lower Manhattan. That budget feel has been transformed into an elegant dining room. I settled in with a classic Sidecar Cocktail as I waited for my lunch companion to arrive.

Our first entrees were Tête de veau ravigotée (fried veal head, sauce ravigote) and Raie au poivron et câpres (Poached skate, capers, sweet pepper vinaigrette). Each was nicely presented and had warm and tender textures. Eating boiled calf's head is a Lyonnaise specialty which I could get used to at Le Coucou. The skate was equally delicate and cooked to a subtle tenderness.

The Quenelle de brochet, sauce américaine (pike quenelle, lobster sauce) replicated as close to the authentic Lyonnais cooking, made out with really local ingredients amongst which pike, usually fished in Rhone Alps streams, and free-range eggs from the neighbouring French region of Bresse renowned for its quality poultry. Freshwater crayfish is another essential element of the quenelle dish since it composes the creamy Nantua sauce, here américaine, traditionally accompanying the pike dumplings.

The Entrecôte Bourguignonne (ribeye, escargot, shiitake, garlic and parsley butter) was another dish created as homage to the Bourguignonne where the sauce was made with a base of red wine with onions or shallots, a bouquet garni reduced, strained and poured over fresh lettuce with escargots.

Our lunch completed, we left the rural dishes of France behind and returned to the crowded streets of Manhattan. Le Coucou made us feel like Americans in Paris, if only for a brief respite.
Nothing French about this restaurant at all Mexicans are cooking the food in back and the food it too pricey for such a small amount

Second time at this restaurant. Food was OK, though overpriced. Service was uneven. Lobster tail was overcooked; dover sole, duck, and venison were fine. Service and staff left much to be desired. Sommelier recommended a wine, which we agreed to, and after being asked a few questions, she politely informed us that she was busy, and would come back later to continue the conversation. Never happened, and it felt dismissive and rude. Our waiter spoke too quickly and seemed disinterested in attending to us. Finally, being seated near the open kitchen (which chef Daniel Rose wasn't presiding over) we witnessed all sorts of ugly friction and public remonstrations by the chef & maitre d. It was really off-putting. If you're going to have an open kitchen, behaviors should be measured and tempered. Given how poorly the leaders of the restaurant were acting, it's no surprise that this behavior trickled down to the staff in general. I should say that we loved Daniel Rose's Parisian restaurant Spring, which had excellent food/service, including an unforgettable moment when a regular couple came in with their small dog, and Chef Rose greeted them warmly, personally bringing a bowl of water for the dog. Maybe one day Rose will grace us NYers with a new, smaller restaurant which better approximates the positive vibes he established at Spring.

Attentive but not overwhelming service. 

Pike quenelle in lobster sauce was very good- quenelle was airy and the lobster sauce was rich and flavorful. 

Monkfish in mussel broth with turnips was excellent. The rabbit was too gamey for us, not as good but was the only miss. Mille fuille were perfect.

Cost was what you would expect for this quality but honestly more than fair by NYC standards. 

The space is simple yet perfect. 
Great traditional French cuisine, old school style with a modern twist.

Love this place! We took our mother to for her 70th birthday, & they were SO sweet & accommodating. The food was out of this world & the service matched. From the moment we walked in, the staff was congenial & professional. Very impressed. We will be back soon. Thanks for making it such a special experience!!

This was our big NYC splurge and worth every penny!  We had an early reservation since we had flown in from a different time zone and hadn't had lunch. We were initially feeling underdressed having walked 2 miles from our hotel in airplane outfits but were immediately put at ease and welcomed to a lovely table. The food was beautiful, not too heavy and very FRENCH-excellent wine list and the somm was terrific. We ended up with a lovely white Bordeaux that we were unfamiliar with but loved and went with all 3 of our meals.  I can't wait to go back dressed to the nines!

Our party of four had a marvelous experience at Le Coucou. The decor is elegant even though the restaurant itself is kind of in an unexpected location in Chinatown.

The service is excellent. We had to wait 30 min for our table past our reservation time, and we all received free drinks as compensation. When we only ordered one hor d'oeurve for our table, our waiter gave us another dish for free just to give us a more complete course. We don't recommend the leek dish, but we loved the special which was egg with uni. Great texture and flavor!

Our entrees were delicious of course. The rabbit came in three parts: 2 meats and a broth. The monkfish included a seafood broth with lobster that tasted amazing with the French bread. The pigeon was perfectly crispy on the outside and tender on the inside.

I liked this restaurant because the chef rewards trying new things. I felt confident ordering meats I would never eat anywhere else here.

For dessert, we had the pistachio ice cream/marshmallow dish where they poured fire over it at the table in front of us to toast the outside. We also had the chocolate mousse and white coffee ice cream. Both were perfect for ameliorating our vet full stomachs at this point. Lastly, the check came with a chocolate, a cookie, and a jelly each.

As far as fine dining goes, Le Coucou is well worth it both for the overall meal and even for the price. The drinks are strong, and the food is deceptively filling. I didn't realize it at first, but the dishes had so many parts that by the time I finished trying everything, I was stuffed. Usually leaving an upscale restaurant leaves me content but still vaguely hungry. Here, I was 100% satisfied with both quantity and quality.

I recommend asking for a kitchen table. It's much less private and romantic, but you get a great view of the bustling kitchen where you can see the magic at work. Every single member of the staff is working 110% here, and you really get the feeling that the they are all here to make your meal the best it can be. 

Highly recommend. Many say that Le Coucou has been snubbed for a Michelin star as they are well-overqualified, and I personally agree. There wasn't one specific aspect that was world-changing, but every single detail here was thoughtfully takes care of with the end result being a top notch evening. We ended being there for over three hours without even realizing it.

Advice:  dont go Coucou over Le Coucou.  The most disappointing evening in a while.  After carefully following the silly one  month in advance  reservation rule we waited 48 minutes to be seated. While the barista was excellent, we should have skipped the overly dramatic, feigned and contrived  service not to mention the fussy food that seemed to make no sense.  The wine was delicious but alsonoverpriced

If you are a true gourmand, you do not have to spend the giant bucks at Le Bernadin, Daniel, Eleven Madison or Per Se. You can have that incredible Manhattan experience of amazing food, service and ambiance at Le Coucou--although it is still not inexpensive. 

Nothing beats a great Manhattan food adventure, not even in France. Le Coucou is the real deal. Enjoy!!!

Gorgeous interior, the pictures don't do justice.  Drinks were good. Didn't have a chance to try the food.  I came here with a couple of friends for dinner without a reservation-stupid yes I know.  However, we called the day before and the day of to confirm and they said they had tables for walk ins and we can come by.  We came, maitre'd told us to wait until something gets free.  We waited for about an hour and a half.  Finally he comes to us as tells us we won't be given a table because nothing is available.  I feel like he should have made it clear that there would be a chance of not getting a table from the get go, we would have understood and not waited.  Restaurant lost a future patron.

Beautiful restaurant, I can't say anything that others haven't said. Big fan of the lunch menu fix.  Peep my pics for descriptions. Other observations.   The handsoap in the restrooms was awesome.
They are on their game.  I was an early luncher, I watched the open kitchen from afar for a few moments, and it was nice to observe. I saw some very simple mentoring and encouraging dish discussions between the head chef, sous chef and line cooks, followed by tasting and feedback. Not a really original thing to see but it was something to make an observation about  but hey, what do I know.   
I know that the service was absolutely perfect and pleasant without any feeling of intrusion or pretentious interactions, always with extreme pleasantries.  I can't wait to return for the pike quinellle.   The hype is for a reason, because this restaurant executes extremely well.

A transportive beautiful experience. A perfect spot to celebrate. The space is stunning with high ceilings and romantic lighting. But omg, the food. 

-The oysters: highly recommend, creamy, light, bright and the nori/seaweed ice was a nice touch
-The leeks: recommend, a unique preparation, tender, light and warm
-Sweetbreads: luxurious and fatty, it was a bit too heavy for my taste, probably would not order this one again
-Quenelle: good lord just get it. I've never had anything like it, so light and unbelievably flavorful 
-Monkfish: highly recommend! Possibly my favorite dish. Very light with complex broth
-Filet de boeuf: it was good, probably would not get again

Not going to pretend to know much about wine but the sommelier gave great recommendations!

Was sad to be feeling too obese for dessert. Next time.

While Le CouCou is definitely a fancy place, they didn't bat an eye when I showed up in a sweater, jeans and chuck taylors (I didn't know I was going to dinner when I got dressed that morning). The place is expansive, but not overly designed. The candles melting onto the white tablecloths definitely give it a romantic sensibility and the dishes all have complicated french names that are a bit difficult to decipher. However, the staff was friendly and helpful and overall the food was incredible.

To start we had the poached skate. I've only had skate one other time and this blew it out of the water. The vinaigrette perfectly complemented the fish which was flaky and tender. Capers and small croutons added a nice textural element on top. Our first entree we had the halibut in a buttery beurre blanc sauce over pickled daikon. The tangy daikon cut the fattiness of the sauce and the combo of flavors was pretty much perfect. Next we had the filet de boeuf - this one is a must have. The meat was cooked to perfection with bone marrow pellets on top. It was served with oxtail potatoes that were so rich they could have been served as a dish on their own.

The sommelier helped us with pairings for each dish and while we didn't order a ton of food, we were full and happy by the end of our meal, mostly due to the overall richness of the menu itself. We capped the night off with a cappuccino each and went home very satisfied.

Let me preface this review by saying that it's not about the food, nor the service, nor the ambiance. 

I had dined at Le Coucou once before and enjoyed it quite a bit, and in trying to select a restaurant to celebrate my birthday at, thought it would be a great choice. I saw that online reservations were limited to 6 guests and followed the instructions to email with an inquiry about larger parties for a la carte dining. The response I got shocked the hell out of me. 

I was informed by the director of events that the only way for Le Coucou to accommodate a larger party is for said party to buy out the entire restaurant on the desired date for a private event. As reasoning for this policy it was explained to me that this was in the interest of providing the utmost service to all diners, and that as such, Le Coucou does not feel comfortable serving both large parties and a la carte diners simultaneously. Now, hearing all of this you might assume that my party was somewhere in the double digits which might warrant buying out an entire NYC restaurant for an evening to host an event, but if you ask me 8 people at one table HARDLY constitutes a large party, and frankly the mere suggestion that U should pay a huge sum of money to buy out a restaurant so that I and seven other diners can celebrate a birthday over dinner is both insulting AND ludicrous. After all, it's hardly some tiny hole in the wall where a table of 8 will dominate the space. 

Put simply, Le Coucou ought to drop that pretentious policy asap because in a city like New York, where equally hyped up newish restaurants and far superior cuisine provide more than theifair share of competition, that s*** will only fly for so long.

The food was pretty good but not worth the price. Our service was good as well other than a mistake on their take of a Baked Alaska where it ended up tasting like vodka. The ambiance reminds you of any other fancy French restaurant as well.

This place is beautiful but learn French before you go. Menu is mostly in French and they are not good about explaining what you order. I end up ordering two fish and they didn't mention I was doing that. The bar tender was the rudest person in the restaurant.

This was a wonderful dining experience. It's hard to strike the right balance in fine dining between quality/professionalism and feeling comfortable. The space had a charming ambience that wasn't too buzzy, but was still energetic and lively. 

The staff here is impressive at both the details of serving a meal and the customer interaction - our main server was so professional, striving for perfection in the slightest details, while also willing to banter with us a little and make accommodations that were necessary. 

The sommelier got it just right in her recommendations and spent the time to talk us through a few options.  

Our meal was truly delicious - favorites included the oeufs printanières and the leeks to start, the filet and the vegetarian main entree option. The deserts (the Omelette Norvégienne is flambé!) and cheese plate were a great way to finish. 

Had a wonderful time and hope to go back again.

My experience here was great! I went for brunch and they had a pre fixe menu. So for the fixed price we got to choose one app and one entree.  I started with some green drink. It was a suggestion of the waitress, unfortunately don't remember the name. For an app, I had a potato soup with creme fresh and caviar. It was absolutely delicious! To the point that I almost ended up licking the plate. For entree, I got a ribeye with escargot. That was also great. It was done in a light parsley sauce, and escargot it always a good idea! Overall, my friend and I had a great experience! Plus the place is gorgeous!
The lunch set is cheap. I love the butter but not the dishes. The sausage is recommended by waiter but not fit me. The caviar soup is great. The environment and service are excellent.

Food is ok but lower than my expectation. Ambience is really pretty. But the service is bad, waitress interpret you while serving food and not the service quality match this kind of restaurant.
May not come again. I thought this should be my favorite place in New York but ruined my fantasy.

Le Coucou is one of the most difficult reservations to snag in NYC so we felt fortunate to confirm a res for Sunday brunch to celebrate a birthday. It was an omen of good things to come. Staff is warm and friendly while maintaining the most professional demeanor. We called to say we were running about 15 minutes late and they reassured us not to worry. They would gladly hold our table.
We tried to balance our food preferences with a desire to try as many dishes as possible. For our first course we sampled Salade Genoise and Tête de veau ravigotée (fried veal head) and both got rave reviews. For our second course we ordered Omelette aux caviar, Quenelle de brochet aux coquillages and Bavette à la bourguignonne. The omelette was light and fluffy, no complaints at all, but not something I'd order again over the many other options. Our server recommended the Quenelle, a dish they are known for, described as pike pureed into a mousse and poached. All I can say is it was like nothing I've had before and absolutely amazing. Also had the Bavette à la bourguignonne which was also a winner. 
All portions were generous and service was exceptional. The restaurant has a serene yet refined ambiance adding to the enjoyment of our meal. Brunch is $54/pp which while pricey was worth every penny. Not only will I be back for brunch again, I can't wait to try dinner and keeping fingers crossed I'll get a reservation other than 5:45 pm.
great food great service great ambience..... the steak was amazing. On my top 5 list. will be looking forward to go again

I just had a great meal at King, which leads me to my experience at Le Coucou the following night. The food was niggardly in portions and uninspiring. I had a tasteless fried eel, an uninspiring rabbit dish, and my wife had a small undistinguished lamb chop. The service people spoke inaudibly and had minimal understanding of, for example, the cheese dishes. The service overall was pretentious but with a poor attitude. The check was thrown down instantly after the desert dishes were cleared. It could be because the four of us were over 60. I just left shaking my head at the experience.
Great food, service and ambiance! Took a long time to snag a reservation with recent time but it's worth it! This place truly lives up to the hype!
I went here for my pre-birthday lunch. The service was great, the cocktails are nice. I'll be back to the restaurant again.

AMAZING restaurant ! Went here for lunch to celebrate my 25th with my mom and had the most wonderful experience with fantastic food and service. Will definitely recommend for fabulous food and a wonderful time !

One of the most memorable early lunch experiences you can get in NYC. 

$54 for a two course meal and exceptional service. 

We each started with their oysters, which were great. 

Buckwheat crepe w/ an egg and a huge, sweet, buttery lobster claws? Yes please. 

How about the beef tartare with all the mixings? Amazing. 

Easily one of the best fine dining spots in the city.

Love the atmosphere and great service! 

As for the food, I expected more. 

Veal tongue with caviar looks great but missing something. I love tongue. And usually try tongue dish but will not order it again. The tongue is very soft and great texture but missing flavor.

Oysters with nori seaweed, it was ok nothing special.

And for the main dish, I think they can do better.

Their wine lists are great! And all the staff working there are very professional and nice. 

We didn't enjoy our dishes as much but it was a nice dinner experience because of the great atmosphere and nice people.

it was spectacular! Four foodie broads did the 2 course lunch and everyone shared one dessert. I can't say it was affordable because when the food is this good it's hard to resist the wines (loved that its a woman sommelier!) but it was certainly doable for a special occasion.

Amazing Restaurant the food is very delicious and the ambiance is just wonderful.  The oysters I think were the best Oysters I ever had.  Everything was delicious. They are very friendly and accommodating. I dined with my Fiancee for her birthday and she just loved it!  Thank you so much for helping me give her a wonderful night!

I had the lunch prix fixe menu here which is two courses (appetizer & main). We were able to try a nice variety of dishes from the menu including the oysters (with seaweed ice, not the biggest fan), potato soup with creme fraiche and caviar (good!), baked eggs (very good, but also very salty), quenelle (appreciated how delicate and unique it was), whole-fried fish (very crispy, well-cooked), and steak with escargot (the favorite of the table). 

Overall, it was an interesting experience trying such traditional French dishes. I was particularly curious about the quenelle since I read it's very uncommon to see in restaurants. It pretty much tastes exactly how it's described: creamy seafood jelly omelette. 

I can tell they use quality ingredients and really care about the food their making. You really have to appreciate and understand French cuisine to have a truly enjoyable experience. The space is gorgeous though and the service was great.

Sorry I cannot share the view of others as "one of the best dining experiences ever" or ".. in the city".

Realize this is one of the higher priced and fine French dining spots in the city. And we had breakfast!

We grabbed a quick breakfast as we were staying in the hotel in the same building.

Go just to enjoy the space - beautiful. Imagine it could be romantic at night.

Service was great.

Coffees are above average but plan on a long wait. Overall - plan on a leisurely breakfast...

The salmon fume was a clear winner, Nothing to write home about the omelette and "Coucou Complete" (egg, bacon, and potato pancake). But what should one expect for breakfast?

Damages with tip for 3 was $85.

Another awesome experience - Le Coucou is solidly one of our NYC favorites. The restaurant's design is enough reason to go through the labors of making a reservation (i.e. waiting until midnight a month out). Once there, you'll find the space is intoxicating, with a real sense of place. It just feels right. Chef Daniel Rose has crafted a menu that is at once classic French, yet sleek and modern. The execution is perfect, and flavors unique and harmonious. Wine list is expansive in French selections, though be careful value-wise. Rather surprised Le Coucou has still not been awarded a Michelin star, as it is every bit deserving. It really is the total package.

Atmosphere:
- Seductive, with tall ceilings, painted brick, perfect lighting and individual candlesticks on each table.
- Bar area is more of a waiting place for your table, not very much seating, so don't plan to linger.
- Dress code errs toward smart casual or above, but we certainly encountered more casual as well.

Food:
We loved everything, yet again! The cuisine is refined and elegant, but not fussy or dainty. Le Coucou's kitchen operates with precision, and it is hard to find any fault in what we had. We really enjoyed the concept, a nice blend of French techniques with a modern viewpoint. Our selections were just the right amount of food for two. We sampled:

- Poireaux (leeks, hazelnuts - $13): One of our favorites, the hazelnuts make it quite unique. Refreshing and super clean.
- Boudin "Les Aldudes" (blood sausage, apple, piment d'Espelette - $21): Rich and satisfying, but the vinaigrette really cut through to make it balanced.

- Crépinette de volaille aux foie gras et fruits (chicken and foie gras, roasted fruit - $28): Succulent and flavorful, the roasted fruit such a nice complement.

- 'Choucroute' à la Juive (Duckling, Foie Gras, Daikon Radish - $98 for two): Excellent, loved the breast and confit; the foie gras sent it over the top. Cooked perfectly. Daikon was prepared like sauerkraut, would have preferred something with less pungent acidity.

- 3 Cheeses (Aretheusa Blue, O'Bannon Goat, Adair - $21): Selected by our waiter, nice job.
- Tarte aux Fraises (Strawberries, Almond, Fromage Blanc - $16): Concentrated strawberry flavor, but not overly heavy. Quite enjoyable.

Beverage:
We started with a glass of the 2011 Philippe Foreau Vouvray Brut ($18), a sparkling chenin blanc from the Loire Valley, which was refreshing and an excellent by the glass selection. With dinner we very much loved the 2012 Domaine du Pégau 'Cuvée Réservée' ($225), a beautiful CdP. The wine list contains an array of French options, but one has to be careful on value, it seems, with some quite decent names though suboptimal vintages in several cases. Found more to my liking in the Rhone and Bordeaux sections. Concluded with some Chartreuse ($25) per our waiter's suggestion, which was enjoyable.

Service:
- Attentive and professional, found it to be less mechanical than on our last visit.
- One of the (very French) waiters assisting our table made some great recs.
- Somm was approachable and knowledgeable.

My visiting parents were staying at 11 Howard last weekend but we were all booked up for our dinners, so we opted to try out Le Coucou for a quick breakfast. Reservations were secured a couple days in advance, but you shouldn't have a problem eating a weekend breakfast here as it ends at 10:30 am and doesn't appear to be too popular.

The space is gorgeous. I can imagine an extremely romantic dinner here, though it was still charming in the morning. Take a picture of the bar on your way in or out and I guarantee you dozens of Instagram likes for your trouble.

Even for a relatively simple breakfast, expect high prices. I picked the smoked salmon plate partially because at $18 the price was comparable to the rest of the menu. The salmon was high quality, with standard accompaniments of cream cheese, toasted bagel, onion, and tomato, though it falls short of the pure joy of Russ and Daughters. My mom's omelette ($16) was good but nothing special, and my dad's Coucou Complet ($15) fared the same.

Coffee is perfectly executed and well presented, though notably strong.

Service was gracious but seemed a bit off. Everything was slowly paced in a way that seemed misjudged-- there's simply no reason to tell us the kitchen is closing at 10 am ten minutes before, and then stand right next to the table while not taking our order for eight of those minutes. Our waiter also asked us the same question twice on three separate occasions.

Overall, I'd like for their breakfast to be a little more interesting given the sky-high prices. I expect they excel at lunch or dinner, when they can luxuriate with rabbit and lobster and such, but there's something lacking about their simple approach in the mornings. I found myself wishing we had gone to Steven Starr's and Roman and Williams' other collaboration, La Mercerie, around the corner, which we toured afterwards for their home goods (alas, no $38,000 bed frames for me), especially as that swoon of a Pete Wells review came out only a couple days later. I suppose there's always future trips as south SoHo has emerged as my parents' favorite neighborhood to stay in.

Never have received such pretentious and rude service upon arriving at a restaurant.  930am breakfast reservation, arrived 925am with plenty of tables open. We were told the "table was being prepared" and sat at the empty bar area.  3 minutes later we asked to be seated given the plethora of tables and were told we were still early for our reservation.

Needless to say we walked out and had a fantastic breakfast in Soho.  Such a shame but will never go back.

After making a reservation one month in advance to eat at a reasonable time (after 5pm and before 11pm) and celebrate my husband's birthday, I expected to have a dining experience commensurate with the restaurant's reputation and fine dining price point. Needless to say, our experience did not match on either count. The food, while very good, did not surpass in quality or creativity other NYC French establishments like Daniel or Bouley. The service (with the exception of the helpful sommelier) was pretentious and unwelcoming.  The waitstaff's impatience with questions about the menu (with vital information in French requiring translation) was palpable, and we were most certainly rushed through our meal. We were seated at 7:30, and our table was totally cleared by the waitstaff just before 9pm. Also, I informed the restaurant at the time of our reservation and upon confirmation that we were celebrating a birthday, but there was no acknowledgment of this whatsoever.  Aside from coming to see the beautiful space, I would not recommend to Le Coucou to anyone unless they are okay receiving subpar service for a meal that is not in itself memorable at all!

I found this is as a good restaurant but not great, the atmosphere and vibe is great but food for the price is just  a ok. Really worth the experience for a corporate dinner or a non special date out dinner. I want to keep like that..

Le Coucou is a beautiful restaurant. And we had one of the best meals we've had this year in their dining room.

About my only complaint was a noticeably long wait between courses. Other than that, everything was flawless- beyond flawless.

I hesitate to describe our individual dishes as I don't believe you can go wrong with anything on the menu. But if you're curious, we had the lobster and scallop stuffed cabbage and the sweetbreads to start. Wonderful...

But the best dishes were our main courses. We had "all of the rabbit" and the duck (for two). I'll just say that the dishes displayed pure mastery of the relevant cooking techniques by the kitchen staff.

The lemon crepe souffle, for dessert, was the perfect ending to our meal.

One of the best restaurants we've experienced in NYC so far...

Fire alarms and fire department the night I attended a private event. Otherwise the service and food was stellar. Gracious atmosphere and attentive staff. The food was inventive, well prepared, plated and most important mouth watering from course to course. Will definitely go back !!

I have eaten at my fair share of fine dining restaurants so I do understand the cost of such an endeavour however considering the price of Le Cou Cou and the quality of the product and service I wouldn't recommend this place to anyone. 

Firstly, don't come here if you want to drink alcohol as you will be paying upwards of around $18 per drink

Secondly, the starters and the desserts are nice and relatively well priced however the entrees (we call them Mains) were ridiculously overpriced for what they were 

Thirdly, don't bother ordering cheese here. You can get better value cheese of the same quality for less at your local grocer. For a French restaurant this was pretty disappointing as was the way they served the cheese (with canned apricots & no quince or similar accompaniments)

We waited for 15 minutes for our table and we weren't offered a drink the entire time. To put this in context there were 2 other people in the restaurant at this time and we arrived at 5pm (the time they open for dinner). 

If I wasn't with my family I wouldn't have tipped as kindly as we did. Quality over quantity (you don't need 100 staff walking around parading food & acting extremely posh, perhaps just one genuine and available server would be ideal)
Excellent- great food and service. Very attentive gorgeous plating. Highly recommended!

Another great New York dinning experience. Ambiance is excellent with soft candle light. We were in the room outside the main room with the kitchen which is quieter and still allows you to see the kitchen without all the hubbub. Definitely where you want to be for a date night. 
Bar is small but appropriate for any table waits as opposed to a stand-alone operation. Also very nice since you can actually find a seat and have a conversation. 
Food and service was also excellent. We had the chicken and foie gras, roasted fruit dumpling, soft shell crab and oysters. All were excellent. Really wanted to try the sweetbreads but that gives me a reason to come back when next in NY. For the main course, we had the Dover Sole and Monkfish, both were excellent. The crepe for dessert was also delicious. 
The service was outstanding and the recommendations from our server were both thoughtful and spot on. The Som was very knowledgeable about their excellent wine list and steered us to a White Burgundy that was a perfect match for our food selections. Just could not have asked for a better more enjoyable dining experience. This is a must try in NY.

DINING SANCTUARY ~
You've  heard it all before.... reservations can/ 
MUST be made 28 days in advance. At 12:15am 28 days in advance I "snagged" (?) a 6:15pm reservation. ABOOK IT. Even the first time there you  are welcomed as if you are a frequent guest. Excellence in food preparation, presentation, and service is paramount. The room,in spite in the intermittent rumbling of subway, is a dining sanctuary

Came here for lunch a little over a week ago with some coworkers and had a good time. Great ambience and service. I struggled between three and four stars, and ultimately went to three because there are places I think are a lot better for the same price range and I felt like the food here was a little too rich, but it could've also been me not ordering the right things.

I started with the Velouté de pommes de terre, which was essentially a fancy potato soup with caviar. As far as potato soup goes, it was good. But how good can a potato soup be? This was definitely me misordering and I may have experienced some envy looking at my coworkers' appetizers! I then had the Caille en salade aux raisins. The quail was cooked well, the foie gras juicy (maybe a little too oily juicy....), and the portion size pretty large. I liked the fresh salad that came on the side but could've done with a lot less bacon. The grapes added a nice touch though. We also shared the Quenelle de brochet aux coquillages, which was rich and creamy. I enjoyed it, but can't imagine eating an entire one.

For dessert, we ordered the rhubarb sorbet, and coffee and salted caramel ice creams. They were delicious, especially the rhubarb (surprising I know). If you're looking for pretty rich French food that will put you into an incredible food coma, Le Coucou is a great spot. If you need to be functional in the afternoon, lunch at Le Coucou is a dangerous game to play.

It's really that good. The service is not stuffy, while on point great. I love the hosts. Nice to everyone.The fish selections are among best I've had. Pricey, so save those pennies and splurge for a nice romantic dinner in a beautifully fully designed space.

I absolutely love traditional French cuisine. It is so hard to find a place that closely can compare itself to France, but Le Coucou has won that spot in my eyes. 

We celebrated our anniversary at this gorgeous candlelit restaurant. Even though I may say some of the dishes can be heavy, it is ridiculously delicious and savory. Every dish was made and presented table side. Something we have not experienced with every dish at any restaurant. 

Ordered:
1. Boudin- I haven't had Boudin since Montmartre at a small cafe, and it brought me back to that day. A little vinaigrette on top of the lettuce, which helps balance out the richness of the Boudin.
2. Whole duckling- This was made in different ways, which is amazing! A very generous piece of steamed foie gras, seared duck, duck heart, and duck confit. 
3. Sweetbreads- the sauce that came with this dish was finger licking good. Don't worry though, we licked it with the remaining baguette bread of course. 

Both my boyfriend and I are picky dessert eaters in general. The omelette Norvegienne that night blew our MINDS! We would go back to Le Coucou just for it, believe it or not! It was an absolute delicious mix of cold and hot, cake and ice cream, sweet and bitter due to the rum. Everytime I think of it, I just want a bite of it already! The presentation was fun to watch with the flambee. 

Another winner in my books. Such a winner that we can't wait to come back here with hesitation! (If we can snag a ressie again that is....)

Best meal we've had in NYC to date. As avid Starr fans, this had been on our list for a while, and we finally went for my 30th. 

We were a little underdressed for dinner (oops!), but were treated incredibly well. The staff all seem genuinely excited to be here, and guided us through the menu and wine list. 

A friend who helped create the menu originally gave us some tips on what to order, and the staff also made great recommendations. 

We went with two items from each section of the menu, and while everything was fantastic, you really, really shouldn't miss the Oeufs printanières, the Chou farci aux fruit de mer, the Sole Véronique or the Agneu de Colorado. We chose our food first, then asked the sommelier for a wine that would pair well. 

Still dreaming about it, and can't wait to go back to try their brunch...

Beautifully decorated restaurant evocative of Paris with the wrought iron windows and old, irregular windowpanes and romantic chandeliers.

Service here was thoughtful and attentive - servers would place a napkin barrier between you and your water glass when they refilled your glasses. The meal started off with a sunflower seed bread and a regular sourdough batard - it was pretty good. My boyfriend and I got the seaweed topped oysters, and they offered to add a fourth since it usually comes with just three oysters. The seaweed ice topping (and a bit of flying fish roe, j believe) combined very well with the oysters.

We shared the duck for two, which was basically a half duck with duck breast cooked medium rare, foie gras, a confit leg, and a white wine braised cabbage. It's a proper fancy restaurant-sized entree (I.e. it's not a lot of food and you'll probably want an appetizer or a dessert to round off your meal. I thought each component of the duck was cooked very well, my favorite being the foie gras and the seasonings on it. The duck breast could have used a bit more sear on the skin, but that's just me.

We got the omelet Norwegian, which is basically a baked Alaska with pistachio and vanilla ice cream. The vanilla ice cream tasted like pure vanilla bean - I could eat it by itself. It was an ok dessert, and I probably would have had a sweetbread or skate appetizer in its place.

Overall, an excellent meal with attentive service and a fascinating French menu that I would love to explore more of.

Simply a spectacular lunch at Le CouCou!  I can't wait to return for dinner.  The two course lunch for $54 is an absolute bargain.  I had the steak tartare and it was one of the best that I have had recently.  The restaurant itself is simply elegant, in a cool, but not too modern way.  A perfect blend of old world elegance with a modern touch.  The service was perfect.  I am not sure why this restaurant continues to be snubbed by Michelin.  In my opinion, it was easily on par with several of the 2 Star options in NY...

My sister treated me to dinner at the place (Walker/Lafayette)yesterday for helping with her taxes.  We waited for a while for our booking because we wanted to have a "sole" dinner.  So, finally it happened last evening.  With all the fanfare, we did it.  But.... the sole dish was somewhat disappointing.  First, I still remember years ago I had a sole dinner while traveling in Memphis.  That has been my reference as far as "sole" goes.   Last evening's was not worthwhile (except for the occasion).  The fish was not soft, in fact my immediate thought was that it was similar to tilapia in texture, and it was not fluffy in that the meat was like compressed.  I've had bassa at a Chinatown restaurant that was more to my liking (softness and the good feel upon entering my mouth).  Well, for the price of $63, plus all the wait for a reservation, definitely it wasn't a cause for celebration.  The staff, of course, was friendly.  For such a higher class place, they'd better be of commendable service, I thought.  Ha, the restroom was unisex, so I found out, as there was no sign, and in the dark I was hesitant.  Inside, it was also too dark in my opinion (for such a place of relief).  Initially, I thought it was my glasses that had not light-adjusted to the brightness yet.  Then, I visited it after eating, before departing.  Same perception.

KenScale: 8.5/10

It's been almost two years since my wife Jun and I had visited Le Coucou, a hit French restaurant behind chef Daniel Rose (who, as a Chicago-born American, made his name in Paris with a modern bistro called Spring) in partnership with restaurateur Stephen Starr. Too often (and sadly), when a restaurant opens in the city and receives all the buzz and accolade, it's hard to see the restaurant sustain that initial success. Part of that has to with notoriously fickle New York City diners who constantly move around to the next big openings. I, for one, am probably guilty, but once I got married, it's become more difficult to check out restaurants as frequently as I used to as I don't have the luxury (or even willingness, thanks to Jun who is a terrific cook herself) to dine out all the time. Another reason that a restaurant loses its momentum has to do with the fact that chefs constantly look around for the next opportunities and therefore do not always pay attention to their existing ventures with the requisite care. At least that doesn't seem to be the case for Le Coucou, which is still chef Rose's only restaurant (although his wife Marie-Aude Rose has her own restaurant in La Mercerie which we have yet to visit), getting a reservation is still as hard as the moment it opened, and it recently entered the World's Best Restaurant list at number 85. I've been meaning to go back to Le Coucou for a while now, and booked for an early dinner table before heading up to the Lincoln Center for a ballet show. And I am so glad that we did, as Le Coucou is still firing on all cylinders.

Le Coucou's French cuisine is in that ideal state between classic and modern. No single dish jumps out at you with some gimmicks, but each dish that you can brings so much satisfaction with careful execution and balanced flavor and texture. Case in point: an outstanding dish of lobster and scallop stuffed cabbage with Pineau de la Loire (a/k/a chenin blanc) sauce. Once you open up the cabbage shell (which I didn't do as elegantly as I should have), you have a mixture of seafood that was expertly prepared, and the addition of wine sauce underneath, which tasted slightly sour at first but over time grew more and more interesting, worked beautifully with it. How about the French classic Sole Veronique, which the server enthusiastically recommended? It was more or less perfectly cooked, and the addition of grapes and champignons mushroom further enhanced the texture of the fish, while the creamy broth underneath was rich but not overpowering. At $63, the price is certainly not cheap, but then a dover sole dish is expensive everywhere in the city, so might as well have a great one, right? It was certainly one of the best seafood dishes I have had in a while. Jun and I weren't initially sold on the other main dish that we had in prime filet with bone marrow jus (as we thought the seasoning on the meat was a bit too aggressive to our taste), but complementing it with the side dish of hearty oxtail potatoes greatly helped to neutralize that sensation. For dessert, Jun and I hadn't had the Baked Alaska last time we had visited, but that was a mistake. The server poured the brandy on top of the dessert to create a beautiful blue flame that lasted for about 15 seconds. The result was a decadent pastry dish with perhaps a bit too much brandy (Jun winced as she realized what she was eating had the potent brandy), but still a very delicious one with pistachio ice cream inside.

As noted above, getting a reservation for dinner tables, especially during prime teams, still requires a Herculean effort. The beautiful dining room that gives you a sense that you're at somewhere special without having to always show up in black ties was still as elegant as I had remembered on our first visit. There is full bar with French-centric wine list to complement your meal (they do make some really good Old Fashioned cocktails). New Yorkers can't seem to get enough of delicious French restaurants (Jun and I still need to visit newcomers such as the above-mentioned La Mercerie and Frenchette from the team that previously worked at Keith McNally restaurants), but when it comes to a restaurant that one must go to explore the rich culinary tradition of this beautiful country, Le Coucou will always stand out to me as a top candidate. May the restaurant thrive for a long, long time!

I mean... writing a serious review for this restaurant is almost a formality at this point.  So I'll start with how the heck I managed to get a reservation.  Important to note that they start taking reservations for a specific date exactly 28 days in advance.  If you're an avid OpenTabler, you may want to log on at midnight the night before.  I made the mistake of logging on at 8am and woke up to everything being gone for the date I wanted.  However, it's a little known fact that restaurants don't book ALL their available tables on reservation systems (there are some exceptions, like Ko), so I called when they opened and was able to get a table for two at 6:15 on a Friday.  Score.  

Yes, Stephen Starr, you know what you're doing.  I love it when I'm in New York and feel like I've been transported to another place due to the decor and vibe of an establishment.  It was like stepping off Lafayette Street and into a beautiful Parisian restaurant.  We were sat in the back corner table near the windows, which in my opinion is the best seat in the house, giving you a clear view of the gorgeous main dining room and the kitchen at the same time.

Drinks:
I started with the In Memoriam, which was delicious, light, and refreshing.  Definitely recommend.  We then moved on to a bottle of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, which never disappoints.  

Food: 
I don't want to go into lengthy detail here.  French cooking is all about technique and everything was technically cooked perfectly, so in that sense, they did an incredible job and provided a memorable experience.  Instead, I'll just write what we ate and my personal preference on how it tasted.  It's also worth noting that I ran out of room very quickly, so I would not recommend ordering this much, but it was worth being able to try so many things.

Poireaux/leeks - delicious, yet not a flavor explosion, if that's what you're expecting.  Leeks are typical French cuisine, so if you're into exploring, this might be for you.

Chou Farci aux Fruits de Mer/lobster and scallop stuffed cabbage - one of my favorite things we ate

Langue de Veau au Caviar/veal tongue and caviar - turns out I'm not a huge veal tongue fan, but this was very good nonetheless

Ris de Veau à l'Estragon/sweetbreads - one of the richest, most delicious sweetbreads I've ever had, including the two eggs that came on top.  Wow.

Tout le Lapin/all of the rabbit - this actually came out separately with what I would describe as a delicious onion cake, and rabbit broth, hence using "all of the rabbit."  This was definitely worth leaving room for, even though I didn't have any left.  Also one of my favorite dishes of the night.

We finished with a French press coffee and somehow found room for the Saveurs du Printemps/poached rhubarb and I'm glad we did.  Definitely recommend trying this dessert - it's light, tart, and beautiful.

Including some photos for your perusal... Enjoy and good luck getting in!

Old style fancy french restaurant in a modern setting. It's surrounded by Chinatown nonsense and stands out for its low key appearance. Attentive but not overwhelming service.  Beautiful space but I didn't think the food was worth revisiting. Be honest, 4 stars only for the spectacular wonderful ambience, not food.

From the ambiance to the service to our meal everything was top notch. My favorites: poached skate, leeks with hazelnuts, sweetbreads, chicken foie gras, filet with bone marrow and the halibut! Not to mention that the sommelier was very knowledgeable and made some wonderful recommendations!

Le CouCou has been on my list for a while and as soon as reservations were posted online, I started clicking a few seconds before the clock struck and was able to get a reservation. I was so excited and I was not let down. I would suggest arriving early to have a craft cocktail at the cute little bar to the right as soon as you enter the restaurant. LCC is so cozy and the decor is French and chic. Almost all tables have a birds eye view of the kitchen and it was so cool watching them at work (another tip). They have their system down pat and so does their waitstaff. Samantha was my waitress for the evening and she was delightful, intuitive, and very accommodating. I dined on the lobster & scallop stuffed cabbage, the dover sole and for dessert, the lemon crepe. All I can say is WOW! All of the dishes were the bomb.com, but the dover sole.......It is simply the BEST you will ever have which is why everyone raves about it. The lemon crepe paired with the citron confit was rich and deserving of slow, intimate bites..I didn't want it to end. The presentation of every dish was ecstatically pleasing as is to be expected at such a top notch establishment.

Are you serious guys??? After we left the restaurant the waiter run out after us and said that there was missing a hundred dollars to our payment (the bill was 420$). We got really surprised as we were sure that we'd given the right amount. Then he added that maybe he made a mistake and he would like to check it again, went back and came again with apologies.....bla bla bla. 
Are you really serious guys? Do you think your customers are stupid and don't know about that kind of stuff the waiters are doing? We just did not expect that from your restaurant. We thought you respect your customers.
By the way, the food wasn't that tasty neither.

I had no idea how difficult it is to get a reservation here, so with pure ignorant luck, my friend and I walked in and scored the one open table designated for walk-ins that night for dinner.  Though slightly overwhelmed by our lack of French vocabulary and panache in fine dining, we had an incredible memorable dining experience - possibly the best meal I've had in my 30 years.  

To better sample the menu, we ordered a few Hor d'Oeuvres to share and experience together.  The Sweetbread dish (Ris de Veau à l'Estragon) had an amazing tomato tarragon sauce that was so rich and decadent.  We finished the meal with a pistachio ice cream flambée that was topped with brandy soaked cherries - stunning.

Meh. Went for a lunch interview and had beef tar tar for lunch. Yea...lunch. I'm not a business suit type of guy and wine for lunch business person and wasn't comfortable with the setting. A great place for tourists and the nyc bourgeoisie.

Superb French food.  Simply unique. Good service. 
Why 3 stars ? Warm glass of champagne is unacceptable in a top French restaurant in NY. 
Then a glass of warm white wine..., come on..., seriously ? And not even a "we are sorry"?

Oysters are heavenly ... baked eggs with morels and wine .... beef with escargot and salad... chicken with foie gras.  Unreal, all absolutely fantastic... good wine selection as well. 
Service is top notch.
I felt in love this restaurant recently.  But is there Any way you can make the service as good as your food? Thanks!!!

+gorgeous space on the edge of Chinatown
+great, efficient service. dishes cans out quickly, water glass was never empty, and extra butter (!!!)
+delicious fries  
+decided I must come here to visit Anna Delvy's favorite restaurant, after reading the article in The Cut

-did not love my main course, quail with foie gras. the salad, quail, and foie felt like 3 separate items taste wise. the salad even came out in a separate dish. strange dining experience 
-menu was in french. my high school french was not good enough to realize the caviar and cream advertised on the menu were actually just garnish to cream of potato soup

We had great dining experience at Le coucou. I've been wanting to go here for a while so I was really excited to celebrate a birthday here. At the moment you enter Le coucou you feel the great atmosphere. It's a very cozy spot with big candlelight in the ceiling. You go here not only for the food but also to experience true fine dining. And yes I have to say the service was fantastic. 

We arrived a little late but called to let the restaurant know that we were running late and it was no problem. We got seated a nice table for two and ordered a glass of wine and a martini. The martini was top notch and the dinner started out well.

As a starter we got the blood sausage and the oysters. My company said the blood sausage was the best he'd ever had. The oyster were presented on seaweed ice. Very good. 

For the main course we had the whole rabbit and the monkfish. The whole rabbit is a unique concept, to be able to try three different parts of the rabbit prepared three different ways. It's 3 dining experiences in one meal. The monkfish is served with lobster and delicious mussel broth. Amazing new flavors. 

There was one miss during our dinner. I called ahead to let them know we were celebrating a birthday and was promised a birthday message and candle for the dessert. Unfortunately they forgot about this. However, the coconut meringue and raspberry sorbet was great. Melted in the mouth. I was just a little disappointed about the birthday miss. 

Overall we had a great dining experience. The service here is excellent and the food is of the greatest quality. A dining experience out of the ordinary.

Boudin Noir, Quenelles, Ris de Veau. If seeing these words makes your mouth water, brings back memories or speaks to you in any way, you will understand why this restaurant gets the accolades. It's authentic French food, not dumbed down in any way, then elevated to a new level. 
I'm really disappointed by people saying there are other cheaper French options, when for real authentic French food like Lyon's quenelles, it is very difficult to find in the US if not downright impossible, and then to have it elevated further surprised us all. We took our friends here who are French, one of whom lived in Lyon for years (we are francophiles and spend all our vacations there) and we were at awe with every dish. Daniel Rose's talent and passion for French cooking amazed us in Paris at his Spring restaurant and Le Coucou elevated our feelings even further. I thank him and Stephen Starr for bringing authentic modern French cuisine to our shores and then again for the unbelievable level of execution.

A group of 12 of us had dinner here, and the setting is beautiful. We were being a bit rowdy and surprised no one asked us to tone it down - I'm assuming it's because everyone was ordering like it was their last supper. My girlfriend had the lobster grapefruit salad and chicken and foie gras and it was great. I ordered the oysters, soft shell crab, and filet with bone marrow. Mine was pretty good as well. The table pretty much ordered the entire menu and everything tasted great.

Wanted so badly to like this place, and some dishes were in fact really wonderful...Specifically would recommend the soft shell crab and the fried veal head. The latter is really rich so best if you have someone to split it with. 

However, I found the tout le lapin (rabbit dish) too salty. The dish was fun with the three different presentations, but I didn't think the entree itself was really anything special. We got the filet with bone marrow as well and it was ok. For a small cut of meat, I've definitely had way better in the city (momofuku ko really stands out in comparison, though I get price point may be slightly different). 

In terms of service, I'm pretty upset that they forgot to stick a candle in any of the two desserts I ordered for my friend's birthday! I had called 20 minutes ahead of our reservation, so not sure how they could have forgotten...restaurant itself is very pretty and I liked the candles (though they burn hella fast ha - they replaced ours twice during our meal). 

Perhaps this place just got too hyped up so I had high expectations. Either way, I probably wouldn't come back for dinner. Have been told brunch is a fantastic experience though so perhaps I'll give it another shot in the morning if I have a quiet weekend.

Le Coucou has been on my list for a while and I am so glad we finally got a reservation which are a bit difficult to come by if you don't strategise a method to make one 28 days in advance of the date you choose. 

Upon entering, the dining room has to be one of the most beautiful I have seen in New York City, the lovely room is well appointed with subdued lighting, flowers, chandeliers, and tapered candles. 

The cuisine is, well, absolutely sublime! 
The American born chef, Daniel Rose was trained in Lyon, France, which is the epitome of haute cuisine in France. Every dish on the menu was stellar.

We throughly enjoyed the Maryland soft shell crab (Crabe Baltimore-Brest), and the terrine of vegetables as starters.
The duckling with foie gras, chanterelles and cherries in a lovely sauce was heavenly.
The filet de bœuf was spectacular as well.
Definitely try the flambée dessert with pistachio ice cream (Omelette Novegienne). 

The wine list is massive and many bottles are quite on the expensive side, but you can find some good bottles under $100 if you search carefully. The sommelier is good at making an affordable recommendation.

The staff was unitrusive, friendly and efficient.
They have lovely uniforms. 

We will definitely return very soon, probably within a month. We cannot wait too long, Le Coucou is excellent!

This is by far my favorite French restaurant in NYC.  My first experience was brunch a little over a year ago.  It was the only time I could get a reservation.  I believe I reserved for lunch a few months later.  The servers both times took the time to explain every dish we asked about, as well as some of the servers favorite.  It is obvious that the staff is well informed of every ingredient in every item offered. Staff was extremely attentive, but not overbearing.

If there was ever a restaurant to discredit the reliability of the Michelin star ranking, it's Le Coucou. The fact that this place doesn't have three stars (or even one star!) is criminal. Some of the lukewarm reviews on Yelp are also criminal. I didn't have a single bite that didn't wow me throughout my evening. Ok, social commentary rant over. Let's start the review! 

Congratulations! After slaving over your computer and pressing refresh on Resy for weeks you've finally scored your 9:15 PM reservation for Le Coucou. Nice! Dress to the nines and head on into a microcosm of an upscale Parisian bistro that totally juxtaposes the dingy streets right outside. Le Coucou is a beautiful restaurant with white tablecloths, dimly lit chandeliers, and a bar that looks like it came right out of a storybook. The service is friendly, informative, and shockingly unpretentious. 

I started with a sweet "Bon Voyage" cocktail which was a beautiful emerald color. For my appetizer, I ordered the quenelle. A quenelle is a creamed fish that's poached. Sounds disgusting. It's divine. It's soft and silky and pillowy and amazeballs. Please order it. The sauce it comes with tastes like straight butter and cream. It's so rich and luscious and it really starts the meal off with a bang. My father ordered the soft shell crab, which was crispy and salty. It was also very good. My sister ordered the morels with eggs which were, again, very rich and very earthy. This is another must order. The lobster hors-d'oeuvres were the best cook on a lobster I've ever tasted. And I go to school in Maine.

Entree time! Woo! Again, I was pretty wowed by everything I tried. The standouts! My lamb was beautifully cooked. You get a chop and the neck. The neck was so tender it almost melted. It was kinda similar to a shank, so don't get intimidated by eating a "neck." You'll be fine plz  chillax. I wish it came with something starchy, however. If you're prepared to truly drop some change, then get the Dover sole. It's simple, it's perfect. Again, the sauce steals the show. The soft white fish is complemented by the sweet yet tart pop of the grape, and the decadent sauce. Holy can i just bathe in that sauce??

Dessert! We ordered the strawberry tart with the recommendation of our v cool and v helpful waiter. It was pretty good. The dough was flaky and there was a strong almond flavor. It was almost like eating marzipan. Maybe I was eating marzipan. Who knows? We also got the omelette. Before you judge me for making a breakfast for dessert play, just know that this isn't any ordinary french omelette...it's is actually a baked Alaska. Torched meringue, flamed tableside which makes for a pretty #sick #vid, and pistachio ice cream. Honestly, the alcohol flavor was pretty strong on it. But I liked it regardless.

Let's recap. A few months ago I spent a weekend in Paris. Le Coucou was the best French food I've eaten this year, and probably the best French food I've ever eaten. Le Coucou is actually one of my new favorite NYC restaurants. I highly recommend you make the effort to come here. It's worth the investment of both your time and money.

Excellent food served in a terrific space with gorgeous design. Possibly overpriced and staff came off as unnecessarily pretentious, lacking warmth and personality. 

We have been wanting to try Le Coucou for a while now and finally managed to find a time to make a reservation. While we found the food to be excellent and for the most part intriguing. For a group of four we tried the lobster, soft shell crab, and chicken foie gras crepinette to start. The lobster was cooked perfectly but provided nothing special to justify the $29 price tag for a few mouthfuls of claw meat and poached asparagus. The truly enjoyed the crepinette and soft shell crab, both were certainly more interesting than the lobster and perfectly prepared.

As a main dish, I ordered the Tout le Lapin (all of the rabbit) which arrived on three separate dishes, all of which offered a unique preparation. The loin was by far my favorite of the three. Rich, salty, and flavorful. The leg is served in a small copper pot in a bath of broth and vegetables. The broth was warm and full of that amazing umami flavor that can only be truly realized by patiently developing the flavors. You can tell this dish was prepared with care and love, it represents the old style French cooking that is at the heart of Le Coucou.

Our biggest issue with Le Coucou turned out to be the service. Our waitress may not have been human. She was cold, stiff and lacked any warmth. I'm explaining the menu, she informed us that the chef recommends ordering an item from each of three tiers of the menu per person. First of all, this is not necessary, especially for a Monday night dinner. We had a party of four that split two Hor d'Oeuves and a Gourmandises before ordering a main dish each. Every person at our table walked out having consumed more than their fill. I could not have ate any more if I tried. Therefore, while I respect that the chef prefers his menu to be consumed in such a manner, I find it far from necessary. Second, upon telling our waitress that we would not be ordering one of each but a few dishes to taste and then our own entrees, she was taken aback and seemed offended. She lacked any sort of warmth and friendliness that I have experienced at so many of Le Coucou's competitors. I see other reviewers had excellent service so this may be contained to our one server but it was a complete turn off and affected our meal by making the group suddenly feel uncomfortable and unwanted. 

Overall, the food is a fantastic and offers a variety of French classics with plenty of space to try new items. The wine list is extensive and relies heavily (as expected) on French varietals, but has offerings for every price range. I do believe that Le Coucou could benefit by toning down their attitude and allowing their diners to relax, but this is probably one of the best classic French restaurants in the city right now.

I booked online. Same day. My booking details never mentioned the no shorts, no hats policy. The host mentioned that it would've been in the email. Why would I read a long email when I had a confirmation through the app that never mentioned dress code, only cancellation policy. See below. Also, it was 5:45, not 8pm and not prime dinner time. Also, you're on Lafayette a block or 2 off Canal, it's hardly the Four Seasons. Who is going to see my husbands shorts. They were also James Perse dress shorts not ripped denim. 
The host was also kind of a dick about it by repeatedly insisting it would've been in my online confirmation, which, see below, it wasn't. We went to Perry St instead; which is way more upscale and they didn't care about the shorts or hat. Really nonsensical. We'd be done eating by 7, 7:30, before anyone can be offended at eating next to someone in shorts.

A few of my French friends recommended this place to me so I decided to try it out. The place is elegant, cute and low key. The one pager menu is easy to navigate and literally everything looks super delicious and thoughtfully made and named. However the wine list is not. I was totally overwhelmed by the wine list but luckily they had sommes to help out. The lady took a look at our food order and asked what I like. It's difficult to nailed down a bottle because we had soft shell to start and for main I ordered the pigeon but my my boyfriend had steak. I asked for a French red not from Bordeaux or Burgundy and was presented with this delicious wine from north Rhône that goes with both the poultry and beef. The dishes are well portioned so we didn't feel stuffed as when we went to Per Se or starved when we went to Dadong. Oh, and I made wishes to a crêpe for the first time!

This was my first stop during a recent trip earlier this year and one I hope to have again one day soon. Le Coucou perfectly embodies French cuisine, flair and all, but with a side of New York chic and sass thrown in. The electric vibe was contagious during my visit. Not uptight nor stuffy at all as some people often fear a French restaurant would be. Instead, diners enjoyed their time while making​ large amounts of wine disappear (guilty), and partaking in borderline​ rambunctious conversations. 

Rows of beautiful dimly-lit iron chandeliers welcomed me as I walked​ to my table. Walls of exposed brick add drama to an otherwise uncomplicated decor. I noticed every table had one single long tapered candle on it. Each one burned at a different level as if to give away the length of each table's stay at the restaurant. Those having dessert had gone through most of their candle. Coincidence?

WHAT I TRIED:

Sweetbreads
Beef Cheek & Foie Gras Terrine
Prime Filet with Oxtail Potatoes
Halibut
Baked Alaska

HIT: All of it. 

How do I even choose one when everything was c​ooked perfectly and with flavors to match? The simply-plated dishes deceived. It was obvious at first bite that much thought, training, and talent went into each one (and -shocker- without any excess tweezer action). The a la carte menu lists every dish in French first with the English​ translation immediately following. You will find items such as veal tongue, rabbit, pheasant, and venison. Chef Daniel Rose takes traditional dishes, gives them a modern nod and then makes them elegant, but still approachable. I also found the portions to be just right​. 

The service received was appropriate, professional, and not overly fussy.

MISS: Can't think of a single thing other that​ I hate living so far away from it. 

I'm not sure why some people complain about reservations (I mean, I know why, but I digress). It's pretty simple, really. Le Coucou is an excellent restaurant. It's going to be full,​ so plan accordingly​. I knew my target date and booked at midnight, 28 days before. If there's a will, there's a way. Figure it out. Not that hard. Try getting into Chef's Table at Brooklyn Fare. Now THAT'S hard! 

I loved it. If this restaurant was at home (South Florida), I'd be a permanent fixture.

P.S. To the NYC Michelin Guide inspectors: Seriously? Get to it! You've definitively missed the mark on this one.

I had made the reservation almost a month out and was running late. Luckily I made it just in time before it was cancelled! Food was 5 stars but the service brought it down to 4. I felt as though I was being rushed through the courses and wasn't fully able to enjoy my meal. I would give it another try though when I'm back in town.

Le Boo boo,
I live in the neighborhood and was excited to try Le Coucou. 
I've rarely been as disappointed with a restaurant of this class in NYC. The ambience was fine but everything else was either average or below. We had a party of 3 and tried a wide range of items on the menu including the filet which came out cold. We also had the rabbit, this to our dismay came out dry. How do you do that we wondered? The morel mushroom dish was average. I cook a few dishes with morel mushrooms and expected that nice woodsy, smokey flavor. This dish was a soup of butter and salt and didn't have any of that nice morel flavor. A true waste of morels. We ordered dessert to try and end the night with something favorable, we were again left looking at each other wondering how this restaurant rated so well? So many other better options in NYC and even in the same area. Augustine on Beekman St. is one of them, it blows the doors off of this place. I guess we shouldn't of been surprised that we were able to get reservations the same day. 
One Yelp reviewer wondered why it doesn't have a Michelin rating?? Seriously?! Here's one reason: our table had a mound of wax from the candles in front of my friend's dining area. We asked politely to remove the wax so a glass or dish wouldn't tip over. The waiter said it couldn't be removed without changing the table cloth. Scrape it off. It's wax. We agreed to move one of our seats. I'm easy going when it comes to this type of stuff if the food is great. If I had known all the food was going to be mediocre I would have been firm and requested another table or walked out.

The most beautiful setting for a downtown French restaurant. Food was divine and the wine list was extensive and well worth the spend - esp given the corkage fee of nearly $100. Everything was impeccable. The only complaint i would have is the sommeliers inability to pronounce French wines and regions. She butchered the regions and the labels which dampened the ambiance and experience a bit.

This was my first time dining at a French restaurant. It's definitely a very classy place. The white table cloths and chandeliers give it a classic feel. The food was absolutely amazing. I have never had foie gras before. It was absolutely amazing. The preparation of the food is what made it so perfect. I would definitely come back

I had very high expectations for Le CouCou. I've heard so many great reviews and it was very hard to get a reservation. However, I was disappointed. Atmosphere and service were great but the food did not live up to the hype. Overall, very overpriced and overrated.

Poireaux ($13) - Leeks and hazelnuts created an interesting taste.

Quenelle de brochet, sauce americaine - I was not a fan of the texture.

Choucroute à la Juive ($98) - Best dish of the night. But not as mind-blowing as I had expected.

Omelette Norvégienne ($17) - Pistachio ice cream, flambée à l'eau de vie Lovely harmony between the ingredients and eye catching presentation.

So I guess there's some big controversy over this place? Rumor has it there was some drama that kept it from getting starred this year. While I think his choice in location is interesting, Starr marvels yet again, and this place is on its way to becoming a staple in nyc. Being from Philly (which Starr basically owns), I was really excited to visit this spot, upon a recommendation from a friend. Everything about this spot, including its exotic exterior was dazzling.

We had a reservation on a Saturday night, and waited for maybe 15 minutes upon arrival for our table. The crowd is definitely a bit older, and dress is business casual, at least.
